Vigilant
vij'i-lant
adj. (watchful, wakeful; required of the bishop, and commanded of every believer against the adversary)
Latin vigilans, watching, from vigil, awake. It renders Greek nephalios in 1 Timothy — sober, unmixed with wine, hence clear-headed — and gregoreo in 1 Peter, to stay awake.

Biblical Definition

The word stands in two lists that ought to be read together. First among the qualifications of an overseer: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2). The office is a good work to desire (1 Timothy 3:1), and the qualifications are almost entirely matters of character rather than gift — only apt to teach names an ability. Vigilance heads the list of dispositions because a man who is not watchful cannot guard anything, and guarding is what an overseer does. Second, the command to the whole flock: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Peter gives the reason before he gives the remedy, and the remedy is not flight: “Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world” (1 Peter 5:9). Vigilance in Scripture is therefore never anxiety. It is the settled wakefulness of a man who knows there is a real enemy, knows the enemy is a defeated one, and does not intend to be found asleep.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines vigilant as watchful, circumspect, attentive to discover and avoid danger.

expand to see more

VIGILANT, a. Watchful; circumspect; attentive to discover and avoid danger, or to provide for safety.

VIGILANCE, n. Forbearance of sleep; watchfulness.

2. Circumspection; attention of the mind in discovering and guarding against danger.

SOBER, a. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; habitually temperate.

2. Not mad or insane; not wild, visionary or heated with passion; having the regular exercise of cool dispassionate reason.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 3:2 — "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;"

1 Peter 5:8 — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:"

1 Peter 5:9 — "Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world."

1 Timothy 3:1 — "This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work."

Modern Corruption

Eldership is selected for competence and platform, and the one list Scripture actually gives is treated as an aspiration rather than a requirement.

expand to see more

The qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are the only hiring criteria the New Testament supplies for the office, and they are overwhelmingly about a man's character, household and reputation. Modern practice regularly inverts this: churches recruit for communication, vision and administrative capacity, and treat the biblical list as a set of ideals that no one entirely meets. The text does not read as an ideal. A bishop then must be is a requirement, and the list includes a man's conduct at home, his relation to money, his temper and his sobriety. Where the list is set aside, the office is filled by men who can draw a crowd and cannot guard a flock, and the congregation discovers the difference in a crisis.

On the other side, vigilant has been enlisted for a suspicious temper that treats watchfulness as a licence to hunt heresy in every brother. Peter's vigilance is directed at a named adversary, and the same chapter tells elders to feed the flock willingly and not as lords over God's heritage. A watchman who spends his wakefulness on his own people rather than on the enemy has mistaken his post. Vigilance guards the sheep; it does not stalk them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nephalios (G3524), sober and watchful — 1 Timothy 3:2, 3:11, Titus 2:2; gregoreo (G1127), to be awake — 1 Peter 5:8, Matthew 26:41.

expand to see more

Greek nephalios (G3524) — sober, vigilant; 1 Timothy 3:2, 3:11 and Titus 2:2, always in a list of qualifications.

Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to stay awake, to watch; 1 Peter 5:8, and the Lord's word in Gethsemane, watch and pray.

Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop; 1 Timothy 3:2, one office with elder and pastor.

Greek antidikos (G476) — an opponent in a lawsuit, an adversary; 1 Peter 5:8, of the devil.

1 Peter 5:9 supplies the posture: resist stedfast in the faith — not flight, and not fear.

Usage

"“A bishop then must be… vigilant” — a requirement, not an aspiration."

"“Be sober, be vigilant” — because the adversary is real and already defeated."

"A man who is not watchful cannot guard anything."
